reading.body:
AI pre-checks promotional material for mechanical faults, but approval stays with qualified human reviewers.

The pattern is a division of labour. AI catches spelling errors, prohibited phrases, missing safety warnings and other guideline breaches, so reviewers start from a cleaner draft. Veeva has built such checks into its PromoMats content system. The judgement calls, claims and fair balance, remain human.

This matters for AI because it shows where the technology actually lands in a regulated workflow. Review queues are a known bottleneck, and the mechanical layer is the part that can be automated without moving accountability. Fair balance, the requirement that promotional material present risks with prominence comparable to benefits, is exactly the kind of call the data leaves to people.

The data does not say how much time the pre-checks save, how accurate the flags are, or how many organisations use them. It covers one vendor's feature set and the review process around it, not measured outcomes.

explainer:
Medical, legal and regulatory review, often called MLR or promotional review, is the process every piece of promotional material passes before use. Medical reviewers check claims are accurate and supported by evidence, legal reviewers check for legal risk, and regulatory reviewers check consistency with the approved label and promotional rules, including fair balance between benefits and risks.

Review queues are a known bottleneck. AI pre-checks catch mechanical problems before human review: missing safety statements, prohibited or superlative phrases, claims without references, inconsistent product names, and formatting errors. That shortens review cycles and lets reviewers focus on judgement calls. The approval decision and accountability stay with the human reviewers.

What MLR review is

Before any promotional or medical material is used, medical, legal and regulatory reviewers check it for accuracy against the label and evidence, for balance with safety information, for legal risk and for compliance with industry codes. Companies review tens of thousands of pieces a year, from web pages and slide decks to emails and conference posters, and the backlog is a familiar complaint from brand teams.

How AI is being applied

The first uses are pre review checks: comparing claims against the approved label and the claims library, finding missing fair balance statements, flagging superlatives and off label language, verifying that references support the sentences that cite them, and spotting material that reuses already approved content and can take a faster path. Reviewers then receive material with issues marked, which speeds their work and makes it more consistent across reviewers and countries.

What stays with people

The approval decision stays with the reviewers, and most companies keep it that way deliberately: an approval is a compliance act with legal consequences. The model also cannot judge tone, context or how a regulator in a particular country will read a phrase. The measurable results reported so far are shorter cycle times and fewer rounds of revision, which is where the backlog came from. The risk to watch is reviewers trusting a clean report and reading less carefully, which is why good programmes track whether issues found after approval change when AI is introduced.
